ESIDIMENI INQUEST

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's been five years since vulnerable and mentally ill patients were moved from Life Esidimeni to unlicensed NGOs in a bid to save money, who, if anyone, should be held responsible?

Unique Selling Point:
Years after the Life Esidimeni tragedy some psychiatric facilities are struggling to operate due to non-payment of subsidies from the Department of Health. They say they are in financial trouble and will be forced to shut their doors.

Summary:
The formal inquest hearing into Life Esidimeni is due to start on July 19 in the Gauteng High Court, Pretoria. The inquest comes five years after the tragedy in which 144 mentally ill patients died after the Gauteng Health Department moved about 1  700 patients from Life Esidimeni facilities to unsuitable NGOs and state facilities in 2016. We speak to families who lost their loved ones, owners of psychiatric facilities who say they are being let down by the department and parents of children battling mental illnesses. Five years after the mental health care scandal, has the department learnt anything from the tragedy? What should be improved? and we ask whether or not the inquest will yield the desired outcome.

Press Release:


Esidimeni Quest for Justice
Six years after inhumane decisions by the Gauteng Health Department resulted in the deaths of 144 patients in need of mental health care as they were moved out of professional care into community-based NGOs, the National Prosecuting Authority is finally set to conduct an inquest in July into precisely how lives were lost. While an alternative dispute resolution process between affected families and the government led to some financial compensation for those who lost loved ones, exact causes of death remain a mystery. Carte Blanche asks to what extent lessons have been implemented within the department to prioritise mental health care and we ask whether criminal prosecutions will finally bring closure.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


VO – The progression of some mental illnesses often results in families eventually being unable to effectively care for their affected loved ones. These families are forced to make the difficult decision to place their relatives in places that offer specialised care.
Christine Nxumalo says they had no choice but to admit her sister Virginia Machpelah into a psychiatric hospital when her Alzheimers worsened.
CHRISTINE - 04:56 And that’s when they recommended Life Esidimeni to us. 05:35 They said for her kind of care, that one was, for them, ideal. 6:09- We could see the difference when she was at life esidimeni. It wasn’t perfect but at least we knew she was safe and she was getting the treatment that she required. It took us a while and we were just getting used to her not living with us and her being at that facility and comfortable with the facility when all of this happened.
VO – By “all of this”, Nxumalo is referring to the tragic events of 2016, when the Gauteng health department terminated its 30-year contract with Life Esidimeni , a subsidiary of the Life Healthcare Group.
The hospital treats people with psychiatric disorders and intellectual disabilities.
In the 2014/15 financial year, the department spent more than R320 million on services provided by the hospital for nearly 2400 patients. The then Gauteng health MEC Qedani Mahlangu said that amount was unaffordable.
To cut costs, patients were moved to NGOs across the province despite concerns that those facilities were under-resourced.
MASA QUESTION 06:25 : And how did you find out that your sister was being moved from that facility to what we know now as some incompitent NGOs?
CHRISTINE - 07:12 I got an SMS on the 30th of June 2016 saying that my sister was being moved on that very day and that she was being moved to Cullinan and that I could phone a number which they provided in that sms but it wasn't working.
MASA: So what did you do?
8:02 - ... there were new NGO’s who didn’t have contact numbers and we couldn’t reach them other than to use phone cell numbers that were never answered so it was a very difficult time.
VO - In the midst of that chaos, Nxumalo received a disturbing call from a woman who identified herself as an owner of an NGO called Precious Angels in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria.
CHRISTINE - 9:39- ...Ethel Ncube called me and said my sister had passed away and had been with her for about 5 weeks - a couple of weeks with her. 11:15- Well I was at the office when I got the call as you can imagine I just... I couldn’t have a conversation. when we got there, we were sitting and had to view my sister's body so we definitely knew it was her.
VO - Nxumalo later discovered that a further eight patients had died at the same NGO, and many more in other facilities.
MASA LINK - Neglected and under-prioratised what will it take to improve the state of South Africa’s mental health care services?
VO - Andrew Peterson is grateful his uncle Victor Truter survived the country’s worst recorded mental health scandal. Truter had been living at the Waverly facility for four decades when he was moved to the Mosego Home in Krugersdorp.
ANDREW - 28:12- He was thin, I couldn’t even recognise him. He had lost his skin, the texture was dry, you know... I could actually literally feel his bones protruding, you know. MASA: He was starved.
ANDREW: He was starved.
VO – Such accounts were shared by families who testified before former Deputy Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke at the subsequent arbitration hearings five years ago.
ANDREW - 29::15 - ... I asked the caretaker why my uncle is like this and why are these people like this? She said we don’t know these people you know. They haven’t even had their medication yet, that's what she said. They haven’t had their medicine.
VO - In his ruling, Moseneke described the events as “a harrowing account of death, torture and dissapearance of utterly vulnerable mental health care users”. He found that the provincial health department’s decision to move the patients was “irrational and unconstitutional”.
Moseneke ruled that families of the victims be paid a little over R1 million in compensation.
VO – As of November last year, concerned politicians reportedly noted that only R6.5 million of the R120 million set aside for families had actually been paid.
A formal inquest into the tragedy will begin on the 19th of July in the High Court in Pretoria. National Prosecuting Authority spokesperson Lumka Mahanjana says that process will determine if anyone can be held criminally responsible for the deaths of the patients.
MASA QUESTION ABOUT WHY IT TOOK SO LONG AND WASN'T THE ARBITRATION ACTUALLY ENOUGH?
LUMKA - 12:50- ... Initially there were two dockets that opened. Those two dockets had to be merged into one and statements had to be taken from everyone involved. Now it’s quite voluminous those dockets that we had to go through and the interviews and the collection of the evidence. 13:19 - ... another process that delayed ...was the appointment of the judge. The appointment of the judge is lengthy on its own but we are here now.
VO - Moseneke recommended that the government outline a turnaround plan for mental health care services in Gauteng.
Provincial government spokesperson Thabo Masebe says authorities have complied with the recommendations and will fully cooperate with the inquiry.
MASEBE - 9:02- ….We will provide any information that is required from us and ensure that if there are officials that are invited to participate as witnesses, to provide evidence, we will cooperate also in that regard.
UPSOUND MASA QUESTION ASKING HIM IF THE GAUTENG GOVERNMENT HAS ACTUALLY DONE ENOUGH.
MASEBE - 11:32- ...there were clear instructions or recommendations that were directed at the provincial government. The provincial government has acted on all of those recommendations that were directed at it. 12:00- We’ve dealt with the issue of officials that were implicated, 12:32- All of those things that we were directed to do, we implemented them.
VO – Section27's Tendai Mafuma disagrees.
TENDAI - 10:23- What the Gauteng health department had to do was to come up with a mental health plan to fix mental health in the province and what they’ve done to their credit is they have come up with a plan but what we haven’t seen is implementation of that plan. 7:15- That department officials who are doctors and members of the HPCSA should be held accountable professionally. That they should be disciplinary actions taken by the department against the relevant people. We haven’t seen that happen.
VO – Despite Moseneke's stern orders, mental health care in Gauteng is still grossly neglected and under-prioritised.
MASA LINK - The San Michelle home spans about four hectares of land, accommodating about 200 mentally ill patients, operating a place like this is costly - from food, water and lights, medicine and just the general upkeep of this facility runs into hundreds of thousands of rands in a month.
VO - Manager Marius Bosman says it is a constant battle to survive financially, particularly when the health department fails to pay monthly subsidies of R4 500 per patient.
MARIUS - 2:15 -...we are dependent on the subsidy that we receive from the department. We get money from the SASSA grants and then about 10% of our income must be generated from fundraising programmes, donations and sponsorships.
MASA 03:55 So, if you had to put a number to it and quantify it on a monthly basis, how much would you say you are spending here?
MARIUS - 3:59 - Our monthly budget is R1.3 million...the payment doesn’t come on a regular basis - monthly.
VO - And...it’s not just money that the facility struggles with.
MARIUS - 7:52 - Often we experience difficulty receiving medication from the state pharmacies and that puts us in a difficult position...we were without psych medication for a period of three months.
VO - The San Michelle home took in patients who were rescued from under-resourced NGOs during the Life Esidimeni debacle. Bosman isn’t confident the upcoming inquest will bring about much needed changes.
MARIUS - 30:58- ...if it’s not based on truth, if it not based on reality then I have my doubts about the success of what’s going to happen....nobody has been taken to task for what happened.Maybe ... maybe there will be justice in this whole process and we are praying for that because it was unfair on the NGO’s.
VO – Families of the patients who died say the upcoming legal process is their last hope for justice.
CHRISTINE - 32:11 The inquest is very necessary for all of us, for proper closure, so all of us are very happy that it’s happening and we only hope the culprits will have their day in court.
MASA QUESTION ABOUT WHETHER SHE WANTS THEM TO GO TO JAIL?

CHRISTINE - 20:04- Oh yeah please. I am. I mean we are not talking about one person here. We are talking about 144. 19:29- ...as painful as it will be and it has been- we need this. ... if we don’t hold people accountable , what stops it from not happening again?


PROMO SCRIPTS:
PROMO ONE
SIX YEARS AFTER INHUMANE DECISIONS BY THE GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT RESULTED IN THE DEATHS OF MENTAL HEALTHCARE PATIENTS, WE INVESTIGATE WHY THESE SERVICES REMAIN UNDER-PRIORITIZED.
PROMO TWO
144 PATIENTS NEEDING MENTAL HEALTHCARE DIED IN UNDIGNIFIED CONDITIONS. CAN AN INQUEST FINALLY BRING CLOSURE?
PROMO THREE
FAMILIES OF PATIENTS WHO DIED IN THE ESIDIMENI TRAGEDY SAY PROMISES OF JUSTICE HAVE NOT BEEN MET WITH ACTION, CAN THE UPCOMING INQUEST INTO LIVES LOST FINALLY LEAD TO CLOSURE?
PROMO FOUR
ORGANISATIONS CARING FOR MENTALY ILL PATIENTS IN GAUTENG REMAIN UNDERFUNDED. WE INVESTIGATE HOW LESSONS FROM THE ESIDIMENI ARBITRATION HEARINGS HAVE BEEN TAKEN FORWARD.

MARIUS - 7:52 - Often we experience difficulty receiving medication from the state pharmacies and that puts us in a difficult position...we were without psych medication for a period of three months. MARIUS - 30:58- ...if it’s not based on truth, if it not based on reality then I have my doubts about the success of what’s going to happen....nobody has been taken to task for what happened.Maybe ... maybe there will be justice in this whole process and we are praying for that because it was unfair on the NGO’s. CHRISTINE - 32:11 The inquest is very necessary for all of us, for proper closure, so all of us are very happy that it’s happening and we only hope the culprits will have their day in court. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's been five years since vulnerable and mentally ill patients were moved from Life Esidimeni to unlicensed NGOs in a bid to save money, who, if anyone, should be held responsible?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Years after the Life Esidimeni tragedy some psychiatric facilities are struggling to operate due to non-payment of subsidies from the Department of Health. They say they are in financial trouble and will be forced to shut their doors.
metadata.Summary: The formal inquest hearing into Life Esidimeni is due to start on July 19 in the Gauteng High Court, Pretoria. The inquest comes five years after the tragedy in which 144 mentally ill patients died after the Gauteng Health Department moved about 1 700 patients from Life Esidimeni facilities to unsuitable NGOs and state facilities in 2016. We speak to families who lost their loved ones, owners of psychiatric facilities who say they are being let down by the department and parents of children battling mental illnesses. Five years after the mental health care scandal, has the department learnt anything from the tragedy? What should be improved? and we ask whether or not the inquest will yield the desired outcome.
